platforms.title: Positional Vertigo Isn't Just About Your Inner Ear
platforms.meta_description: Recurring positional vertigo often gets blamed on the inner ear alone. A 2020 randomized trial found vitamin D status plays a measurable role too.
platforms.body_html:
If the room suddenly spins for a few seconds every time you roll over in bed or tip your head back to look up, you may be dealing with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV. It's the most common cause of vertigo, and it happens when tiny calcium carbonate crystals called otoconia come loose from their normal spot in the inner ear and drift into one of the fluid-filled semicircular canals that sense head movement. Every time you shift position, the crystals slosh around and send a false signal to your brain that you're spinning. Most people get it treated with a simple in-office maneuver, but a lot of patients find it keeps coming back months later — and the inner ear itself usually isn't the only reason why.

Why BPPV Keeps Coming Back

Because those crystals are made mostly of calcium, researchers have long suspected that calcium and vitamin D metabolism might affect how often BPPV recurs. A multicenter randomized controlled trial published in the journal Neurology in 2020 tested this directly: after treating confirmed BPPV with standard repositioning maneuvers, patients whose blood vitamin D level was below 20 ng/mL were assigned to either vitamin D (400 IU) plus calcium (500 mg) twice daily for a year, or routine follow-up alone. Over that year, the supplemented group had a lower recurrence rate — 37.8% had a repeat episode compared to 46.7% in the group that didn't get supplements, and their annual recurrence rate was about 24% lower overall. That's a meaningful drop, but it's worth being precise about what it means: the benefit showed up specifically in people who started out with low vitamin D, not in everyone with BPPV, and supplementing doesn't replace the repositioning maneuver itself — it lowers the odds of a repeat episode afterward.

Skip the Guesswork — Here's What Actually Helps

The first step isn't buying a supplement bottle — it's finding out where you actually stand. A simple blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the standard marker doctors use, tells you whether you're in the low range the trial focused on. The US National Institutes of Health's Office of Dietary Supplements sets the general recommended intake at 600 IU (15 mcg) per day for adults up to age 70, rising to 800 IU (20 mcg) for adults over 70, largely because skin becomes less efficient at making vitamin D from sunlight with age. Fatty fish like salmon and mackerel, egg yolks, and fortified milk or orange juice are the main food sources; brief, unprotected sun exposure on the arms and legs a few times a week also helps the body produce its own, though that has to be balanced against skin cancer risk, so it's not a substitute for sunscreen on a daily basis. If your vertigo has already been treated once and you're worried about it returning, ask your doctor for a vitamin D test before assuming another repositioning session is your only option — and if episodes come back frequently, get checked for other causes too, since not every recurring spinning sensation is BPPV.

So the next time positional vertigo hits, the real question isn't just which side you slept on — it's when you last had your vitamin D checked.
